questions.question: An API returns HTTP 500. What does `await fetch(url)` do?
options: Resolves with a Response whose ok is false and status is 500
questions.explanation: fetch only rejects when no HTTP response arrives (network failure or abort). Error statuses resolve normally, so you must check res.ok yourself.

questions.question: How do you stop a fetch from waiting more than 2 seconds?
options: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }), then handle the TimeoutError
questions.explanation: fetch has no timeout option. AbortSignal.timeout creates a signal that aborts after the delay, and the fetch rejects with an error named TimeoutError.

questions.question: Which response should a retry helper NOT retry?
options: A network error where fetch rejected with TypeError: fetch failed
questions.explanation: 4xx errors such as 400, 404 and 422 mean the request itself is wrong, so repeating it will fail again. 429, 5xx and network errors are usually transient.

questions.question: Why is blindly retrying a timed-out `POST /payments` dangerous, and what is the usual fix?
options: POST bodies cannot be resent; use GET instead
The first attempt may have succeeded, so a retry could charge twice; send an idempotency key so the server can detect duplicates
Retries are always blocked by CORS
There is no danger as long as you use exponential backoff
questions.explanation: A timeout does not mean the server failed. POST is not idempotent, so payment APIs accept an idempotency key that makes repeated requests safe.
